name: Quizlet
tagline: Flashcard study app with shared study sets, quiz modes, and spaced repetition.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The study engine is one of the most solved problems in software: cards, a scheduler, a few quiz modes, a progress chart. An agent will hand you a working local flashcard app with spaced repetition in a single session, and for your own material it will be better than Quizlet because nothing is gated or ad-wrapped. The gap is everything you did not type yourself: Quizlet's pull is that someone in your exact course already made the set, and that corpus is not something you build. Also missing: polished mobile apps, offline sync across devices, and the audio and image handling that makes language study bearable. Build it if you write your own cards, keep paying if you came for other people's.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you create decks, import CSV, and drill cards through an FSRS-style scheduler with flip, multiple choice, and typed-answer modes plus a per-deck progress view.
requirements: A place to put your own cards, typed or CSV-exported from somewhere else
Optional: a TTS API key if you want audio prompts
whatYouLose: The shared library of millions of user-made sets for your specific textbook or course
Mobile apps with offline study and cross-device sync
Classroom features: teacher-assigned sets, Live games, class progress
The polish of a decade of A/B testing on study modes
moatNotes: The sets are user-generated, which means the moat compounds every semester and no new app can bootstrap it by being better designed.
whyPeopleStillPay: Most Quizlet users are not looking for a scheduler, they are looking for a set. Searching a course name and finding 400 cards someone already made the night before an exam is the whole product, and that search result does not exist on your laptop. The paid tier mostly removes ads and unlocks study modes, which is a mild upsell on top of free access to the corpus. If you are the kind of person who makes their own cards, you were always better served by Anki or a local build; if you are cramming someone else's deck, you stay.
notes: The scheduler is an afternoon, the library is a decade of students uploading their homework.
prompt:
Build a local-first flashcard study app called "Decks". No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Vite + React + TypeScript for the UI
- A small Express server in the same repo for the API
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/decks.db, created and migrated on first run
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- One command to run everything: npm run dev starts server and client together

Data model:
- decks: id, name, description, created_at
- cards: id, deck_id, front, back, notes, created_at
- reviews: id, card_id, reviewed_at, rating (again/hard/good/easy), scheduled_interval_days, ease, due_at

Scheduling:
- Implement a simplified FSRS/SM-2 hybrid in a single pure module src/lib/scheduler.ts with unit tests via vitest
- New cards start in a learning queue with short steps, graduated cards get interval * ease adjusted by rating
- Due cards are selected by due_at, with a configurable daily new-card cap per deck

Screens:
1. Deck list with due counts and a 30-day review heatmap
2. Deck editor: add, edit, delete cards inline; CSV import (front,back,notes) and CSV export
3. Study view with three modes: flip, multiple choice (distractors pulled from other cards in the deck), typed answer with fuzzy match that ignores case, punctuation, and leading articles
4. Stats page per deck: accuracy over time, cards by maturity, retention estimate

In scope: keyboard-driven study (space to flip, 1-4 to rate), dark mode, full offline operation, a seed script that loads one sample deck.
Out of scope: user auth, sharing, mobile apps, image or audio attachments, any public set search.

Put any optional keys in .env with a .env.example. Write a README with setup, the scheduler's rules in plain English, and how to back up the SQLite file.
